title: Dark patterns in numbers
heading: How far off is your gut?
intro: Eight real numbers about deceptive design online: how common it is, what regulators have done about it, and what happens when choices are made fair.
Every figure is real and sourced. Bet on how sure you are.

outro.heading: Design choices have consequences.
paras: Regulators are now treating interface design as something companies can be fined for, and researchers keep measuring how common deceptive design is.
Today you'll look closely at a problem. Be as careful with the evidence as you were with your bets.

questions.q: In early 2024 consumer authorities from 26 countries checked 642 subscription websites and apps. What share used at least one possible dark pattern?
questions.explain: Nearly 76% used at least one possible dark pattern, and nearly 67% used several. The most common were hiding or delaying key information, such as the real price, and pre-selected options.
questions.source: ICPEN international review, reported by the US FTC, July 2024

questions.q: A 2020 study checked the cookie pop-ups on top UK websites that used the five most popular consent tools. What share met the minimum requirements of EU data law?
questions.explain: Only 11.8% met minimal requirements based on EU law, such as no pre-ticked boxes and refusing being as easy as accepting. The study also found that removing the 'reject' button from the first screen raised consent by 22–23 percentage points.
questions.source: Nouwens et al., 'Dark Patterns after the GDPR', CHI 2020

questions.q: In December 2025 the EU issued its first fine under the Digital Services Act, partly because X's paid blue tick deceived users. How much was it?
questions.explain: The Commission fined X €120 million on 5 December 2025. It said anyone could buy a 'verified' tick without real checks, which misleads users about who they're dealing with. X has appealed to the EU's General Court.

questions.q: In 2022 the US FTC said Fortnite's design tricked players, including children, into unwanted purchases. How much did Epic Games agree to pay back to customers?
questions.explain: Epic agreed to $245 million in refunds over design tricks and billing practices that led to unwanted purchases, plus a separate $275 million penalty over children's privacy. The FTC also said Epic blocked some customers from content they had already paid for.

questions.q: In 2021 Apple made every app ask 'Allow tracking?' with two equally clear buttons. In the first weeks, what share of US users allowed tracking?
questions.sub: of US users opted in (Flurry estimate, first weeks)
questions.explain: Flurry reported that only about 4% of US users were allowing tracking in the first two weeks (about 12% worldwide). When saying no was as easy as saying yes, almost everyone said no.

questions.q: Since April 2025, how large a fine can the UK's Competition and Markets Authority impose itself for breaking consumer law, for example with misleading online design?
questions.explain: Under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act, since 6 April 2025 the CMA can fine firms up to 10% of global turnover (or £300,000 if higher) without going to court. Before, it had to take companies to court.
questions.source: UK Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024; CMA, April 2025

questions.q: A 2019 Princeton study crawled about 11,000 shopping websites. On roughly what share did it find dark patterns, such as fake countdown timers?
questions.explain: It found 1,818 dark patterns on 1,254 sites, about 11%, including countdown timers that reset or kept the offer after they ran out. The researchers called this a lower bound, because their crawler could only spot some types.
questions.source: Mathur et al., 'Dark Patterns at Scale', Princeton University, CSCW 2019

questions.q: In 2022 France's data regulator, the CNIL, fined Google because rejecting cookies took more clicks than accepting them. How much was the fine?
questions.explain: The CNIL fined Google €150 million and Facebook €60 million. On Google, accepting took one click but refusing took several; the CNIL said refusing must be as easy as accepting.
